rulings.reason: Rule 3 and rule 5. Codenames are not always-redact items under rule 1; they are ruled case by case. The codename identifies which checkpoint each eval, waiver and release belongs to. Redacting it would stop readers from matching waivers and evals to the right release, so the violation could not be checked. The harm of disclosure is minor, because it only reveals an internal project label.

Rule 3 and rule 5. A codename is not an always-redact item. It is the key that ties registry ownership, waivers, evals and releases to one checkpoint. Removing it would destroy evidence such as the waiver for another checkpoint, the waiver signed after release, and the red-team report. The disclosure harm is low.

Rule 3 and rule 5. A codename is not an always-redact item. It is needed to see that waivers and evals for this checkpoint do not match the release. Redaction would remove evidence, and the harm of disclosure is only a revealed internal label.

Rule 3 and rule 5. A codename is not an always-redact item. It links the registry, the team lead, the waivers, the evals and the new-weights releases. Redacting it would make the finding unverifiable. The disclosure harm is low.

Rule 1. Employee names are always redacted, and the harm is exposing a staff member's identity. This waiver (W-7991) is for a demo booth, and the log ID, timestamp and clause stay intact, so the evidence is unaffected.

Rule 1 requires redacting the employee name, with the harm of exposing staff identity. Rule 3 requires the evidence to keep its property, since the lead of keel signing waivers matters to whether a waiver came from the owning team's lead. Use a consistent pseudonym so the roles can still be compared. Apply the same placeholder in LOG-0006 and wherever the name appears.

Rule 1 requires redacting the employee name, with the harm of exposing staff identity. Rule 3 requires keeping who signed distinguishable, since the lead of ridge signing waivers for other teams' projects is evidence. Use a consistent pseudonym everywhere.

Rule 1. The username identifies an employee, and disclosing it would expose their identity. Use the same pseudonym as the name so the log stays coherent. The log ID and timestamp are unchanged.

Rule 4 and rule 5. The codename is not confidential enough to redact, and it must stay consistent with the other Project Cinder lines. Redacting only the codename would not hide a training approach in any case, and the training-approach claim is not an always-redact detail. The job name carries no hyperparameters or data mix, so the least coarsening is none. Disclosing it causes little harm. Keep the original text.
